sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
This topic covers what civil works are built from: concrete, asphalt, steel, aggregate and wood. Questions ask how a mix is proportioned, how a material is tested and what the test result means.

Much of it is recognising which test goes with which property and reading a stress-strain curve.
pitfalls: Confusing the water-cement ratio (by mass) with a volume ratio.
Using a cylinder diameter as if it were the radius when computing area.

bridge.plain: This topic covers what concrete, asphalt, steel, aggregate and wood are made of, how their quality is tested, and how they behave under load.
core: Concrete is cement, water and aggregate; less water for the same cement means stronger concrete.
Asphalt mix is aggregate glued with asphalt binder, with a little air left in it.
A stress-strain curve from a tension test gives stiffness, yield strength, ultimate strength and ductility.
bridge.links: Structural design uses these strengths; pavement design in transportation uses the mix properties; geotechnics uses the same density and moisture ideas for soil.
bridge.exam: Many questions only ask which test measures which property.

sections.title: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
sections.body:
Concrete is cement, water, sand and stone. The water-cement ratio, by mass, controls strength and durability: less water gives stronger concrete but makes it harder to place. Mix design by absolute volume fills one cubic metre with the volumes of each ingredient plus air.

Asphalt concrete is aggregate glued with asphalt binder. Its design balances binder content against air voids: too little binder and the mix ravels, too much and it ruts and bleeds. Air voids of about 4% are the usual target.
pitfalls: Using volume instead of mass for the water-cement ratio.
Turning a percentage into the wrong factor: 0.5% absorption is a factor of 1.005, not 1.5.

example.problem: A mix has 200 kg of water and a w/c ratio of 0.50. How much cement is needed, and what volume does it occupy at a specific gravity of 3.15?

ideas.title: Saturated surface-dry
ideas.text: At the saturated surface-dry condition an aggregate's pores are full and its surface is dry, so it neither takes water from the mix nor adds any. Mix designs assume that state. Moisture beyond it is free water that raises the water-cement ratio, and drier aggregate soaks up mix water.

ideas.title: Correcting the batch water
ideas.text: Oven-dry weight is the saturated surface-dry weight divided by (1 + absorption). Stockpile weight is the oven-dry weight times (1 + moisture content). The difference between the stockpile weight and the saturated surface-dry weight is the free water, which is taken off the design water.

ideas.title: Water added on site
ideas.text: The most water a load may contain is the maximum water-cement ratio times the cement in the truck. Subtract what was batched to find what can still be added. To raise slump without raising the ratio, use a water-reducing admixture.

ideas.title: Asphalt aggregate is dried
ideas.text: Aggregate for hot mix asphalt is heated until dry so that the binder bonds to it. Water is not a mix design variable for asphalt.

ideas.title: Water-cement ratio
ideas.text: The water-cement ratio is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement. It is the main control on concrete strength and durability: a lower ratio gives stronger, less permeable concrete but less workability.

ideas.title: Water-cement ratio
ideas.text: In the absolute volume method each ingredient's volume is its mass divided by (specific gravity × density of water). The absolute volumes of cement, water, aggregates and air must add up to one cubic metre.
Asphalt content is normally expressed as binder mass over total mix mass, not over aggregate mass. The two bases give different numbers, so check which one a specification uses.

ideas.title: Water-cement ratio
ideas.text: Mix designs assume saturated surface-dry aggregate. Moisture beyond the absorption is free water that would raise the water-cement ratio, so it is found and taken off the batch water.

ideas.title: Water-cement ratio
ideas.text: The water-cement ratio is by mass. The most water the load may hold is the maximum ratio times the total cement in the truck; anything already batched counts against it.

examples.problem: A concrete mix uses 175 kg of water and 390 kg of cement per cubic metre. What is the water-cement ratio?
examples.idea: The water-cement ratio is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement. It is the main control on concrete strength and durability: a lower ratio gives stronger, less permeable concrete but less workability.

examples.problem: A concrete mix contains 380 kg of cement per cubic metre. The specific gravity of cement is 3.15. What volume does the cement occupy?
examples.idea: In the absolute volume method each ingredient's volume is its mass divided by (specific gravity × density of water). The absolute volumes of cement, water, aggregates and air must add up to one cubic metre.

examples.problem: An asphalt mix sample has a total mass of 1,250 g, of which 65 g is asphalt binder. What is the asphalt content by total mass of mix?
examples.idea: Asphalt content is normally expressed as binder mass over total mix mass, not over aggregate mass. The two bases give different numbers, so check which one a specification uses.
examples.steps: P_{b} = \frac{65}{1,250} × 100 = 5.20%. By mass of aggregate it would be \frac{65}{1,185} × 100 = 5.49%.

examples.problem: A concrete batch calls for 760 kg of sand in the saturated surface-dry condition. The stockpiled sand has a total moisture content of 4.6% and an absorption of 1.1%. How much free water does that sand bring into the batch?
examples.idea: Mix designs assume saturated surface-dry aggregate. Moisture beyond the absorption is free water that would raise the water-cement ratio, so it is found and taken off the batch water.
examples.steps:
Oven-dry mass = \frac{760}{1 + 0.011} = 751.7 kg.

Stockpile mass = 751.7 × (1 + 0.046) = 786.3 kg.

Free water = 786.3 - 760 = 26.3 kg.

examples.problem: A truck carries 7.0 m^{3} of concrete with 360 kg of cement per cubic metre. The maximum water-cement ratio is 0.44, and 1,050 kg of water has been batched. How much more water may be added on site?
examples.idea: The water-cement ratio is by mass. The most water the load may hold is the maximum ratio times the total cement in the truck; anything already batched counts against it.
examples.steps:
Cement in the truck = 360 × 7.0 = 2,520 kg.

Allowable water = 0.44 × 2,520 = 1,108.8 kg.

May still be added: 1,108.8 - 1,050 = 58.8 kg.

examples.problem: A concrete batch contains 350 kg of cement (specific gravity 3.15), 172 kg of water, 715 kg of sand (2.65) and 1,100 kg of coarse aggregate (2.70). Ignoring air, what volume of concrete does it make?
examples.idea: The absolute volume method adds the solid volume of each ingredient: mass divided by (specific gravity × 1,000 kg/m^{3}). The bulk volumes of the piles do not add, because the fines fill the gaps between the coarse particles.

sections.deep:
Concrete mix design proportions cement, water, aggregate and air to reach a target strength, workability and durability. The water-cement ratio is the governing variable: lower means stronger and less permeable. The absolute volume method sets the amounts so that the solid volumes of all ingredients add up to one unit volume of concrete, using each material's specific gravity.

Aggregate moisture matters because aggregates wetter than saturated-surface-dry add water to the mix and drier ones absorb it. Asphalt mix design selects the binder content that gives the target air voids, with checks on voids in the mineral aggregate and voids filled with asphalt.
method: Start from the required water-cement ratio and water content to get the cement content.
Convert each mass to absolute volume: mass / (specific gravity × density of water).
Subtract the known volumes, including air, from the unit volume to find the remaining aggregate volume.
Convert that volume back to mass.
Adjust batch water for aggregate moisture above or below the saturated-surface-dry condition.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A mix design is a recipe. For concrete it sets the cement, water, sand and stone for one cubic metre; the ratio of water to cement controls strength. For asphalt it sets the binder content and the small amount of air left after compaction.
terms: mass of water divided by mass of cement in concrete; lower ratios give stronger concrete
the small pockets of air in a compacted asphalt mix, as a percentage of its volume
density of a substance divided by the density of water; it has no units
the condition of aggregate whose pores are full of water but whose surface is dry

sections.title: Test methods and specifications
sections.body:
Every construction material has standard tests that measure the property that matters for it. Fresh concrete is checked for workability with a slump cone and hardened concrete for compressive strength by crushing cylinders. Metals are pulled in tension for strength and ductility, struck with a pendulum (Charpy) for toughness, and indented (Rockwell, Brinell) for hardness. Aggregates are sieved for gradation and tumbled (Los Angeles abrasion) for wear. Asphalt mixes are tested for stability and flow (Marshall).

Specifications name a grade and its minimum properties. Grade 60 rebar yields at 60 ksi. A36 steel yields at 36 ksi.
pitfalls: Confusing hardness (resistance to indentation) with toughness (energy absorbed before fracture).

ideas.title: Why mixes are designed above the specified strength
ideas.text: Test results scatter, so a mix whose average strength equalled the specified strength would fail half its tests. Mixes are proportioned for a mean well above the specified value so that only a small share of results falls below it.

ideas.title: Fresh and hardened concrete
ideas.text: Slump measures workability. Air content is measured by the pressure or volumetric method. Compressive strength comes from cylinders, normally at 28 days. The split-cylinder test gives tensile strength and a beam test gives the modulus of rupture.

ideas.title: Steel
ideas.text: A tension test gives yield strength, ultimate strength, modulus of elasticity and percent elongation. Common grades: A36 with a yield of 250 MPa (36 ksi), A992 with 345 MPa (50 ksi), and Grade 60 reinforcing bar with 420 MPa (60 ksi).

ideas.title: Hardness and impact
ideas.text: Brinell and Rockwell tests measure resistance to indentation and correlate with tensile strength. The Charpy impact test measures the energy absorbed in fracture, which indicates toughness and locates the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.

ideas.title: Soils and aggregates
ideas.text: Sieve analysis gives gradation. The Proctor test gives maximum dry density and optimum moisture content. Atterberg limits describe plasticity. The Los Angeles abrasion test measures aggregate toughness, and the CBR test measures subgrade strength.

ideas.title: Asphalt
ideas.text: Marshall testing reports stability and flow. Superpave binders carry a performance grade written PG high-low, the pavement temperatures in degrees Celsius between which the binder is expected to perform.

ideas.title: Who writes the standards
ideas.text: ASTM and AASHTO publish test methods and material specifications. ACI and AISC publish the design specifications for concrete and steel.

examples.problem: In a splitting tensile test, a concrete cylinder 150 mm in diameter and 300 mm long fails at a load of 205 kN applied along its length. What is its splitting tensile strength?
examples.idea: Loading a cylinder along two opposite lines sets up nearly uniform tension across the loaded diameter. The splitting tensile strength is 2P / (π L D).

examples.problem: A 150 mm square concrete beam is tested in third-point loading on a span of 450 mm and breaks in the middle third at a total load of 28.0 kN. What is its modulus of rupture?
examples.idea: Third-point loading puts a constant moment of P L / 6 across the middle third. Dividing by the section modulus, b d^{2} / 6, gives the modulus of rupture R = P L / (b d^{2}).

examples.problem: A sieve analysis of sand gives cumulative percentages retained on the six standard sieves from No. 4 to No. 100 of 4, 16, 36, 58, 82 and 96. What is the fineness modulus?
examples.idea: The fineness modulus is the sum of the cumulative percentages retained on the standard sieves, divided by 100. A larger value means a coarser sand; concrete sands usually fall between 2.3 and 3.1.

examples.problem: An aggregate sample has a mass of 883.7 g in the saturated surface-dry condition and 870.6 g after oven drying. What is its absorption?
examples.idea: Absorption is the water an aggregate holds inside its pores when saturated surface-dry, as a percentage of its oven-dry mass.

examples.problem: A coarse aggregate sample has a mass of 1,985 g saturated surface-dry in air and an apparent mass of 1,240 g when submerged in water. What is its bulk specific gravity (SSD)?
examples.idea: By Archimedes' principle the loss of mass in water equals the mass of water displaced, which gives the sample's bulk volume. Specific gravity is the SSD mass divided by that loss.

sections.deep:
Standard tests exist so that a material property means the same thing on every project. Each test targets one property under fixed conditions: specimen size, loading rate, temperature and age. Knowing which test gives which property is what the exam asks.

Specifications then state the required result, such as a 28-day compressive strength or a minimum yield strength. Acceptance is statistical: individual results scatter, so specifications are written around averages and allowable low results.
method: Identify the property in question: strength, stiffness, hardness, toughness, workability or gradation.
Note the conditions that affect the result, such as age for concrete or temperature for impact tests.
Convert the test reading to the property with the correct area or gauge length.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Materials are accepted on the basis of standard tests. Each test measures one property: a cylinder break gives concrete strength, a slump test gives workability, a tension test gives a metal's strength and ductility, a sieve analysis gives the range of particle sizes.
needs: Mechanics of Materials: Stresses and strains
terms: the stress at which a metal stops springing back and starts to deform permanently
the stiffness of a material: stress divided by strain while the material still springs back

sections.title: Physical and mechanical properties
sections.body:
The stress-strain curve tells a material's story. The straight first part is elastic: unload and it springs back. Its slope is the modulus of elasticity, the stiffness. The yield point is where permanent stretching begins. The peak is the ultimate strength. The total stretch at fracture is the ductility, and the whole area under the curve is the toughness.

Steel is strong in tension and compression and is ductile. Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, which is why it is reinforced. Wood is stronger along the grain than across it.
pitfalls: Reading yield strength where ultimate strength is asked, or the reverse.

example.problem: A bar stretches elastically by 0.0015 strain under 300 MPa. What is its modulus of elasticity?

ideas.title: Reading a stress-strain curve
ideas.text: The slope of the first straight part is the modulus of elasticity; take it between the origin and a point that sits cleanly on the grid. Yield is where the curve leaves that line, ultimate strength is the peak and rupture is the end of the curve.

ideas.title: Ductile and brittle
ideas.text: A ductile material deforms a great deal before it breaks, which gives warning. A brittle one follows a nearly straight line and then snaps. Bending a paper clip shows yielding: a small bend springs back, a large one stays, and the bent spot has strain-hardened so it resists being bent straight again.

ideas.title: Concrete in compression
ideas.text: Concrete's curve bends over because microcracks reduce its stiffness as load rises. It is close to linear up to about half its strength, peaks at a strain near 0.002 and crushes near 0.003. Reinforcement carries the tension once the concrete cracks; it does not stop the cracking.

ideas.title: Wood is orthotropic
ideas.text: Wood's properties differ along three perpendicular directions, set by the grain. Steel is isotropic: the same in every direction.

ideas.title: Compressive strength
ideas.text: Compressive strength is the failure load divided by the loaded cross-sectional area of the cylinder. Newtons over square millimetres gives MPa.

ideas.title: Hooke's law
ideas.text: On the linear part of the stress-strain curve Hooke's law applies: stress = E × strain. The modulus of elasticity is the slope of that line and measures stiffness, not strength.

ideas.title: Modulus of elasticity
ideas.text: The stiffness of normal-weight concrete rises with the square root of its compressive strength, so doubling the strength raises the modulus by only about 41%.

ideas.title: Percent elongation
ideas.text: Percent elongation is the permanent increase in gauge length at fracture divided by the original gauge length. It is a measure of ductility, along with reduction of area.

examples.problem: A 150 mm diameter concrete cylinder fails at a load of 710 kN in a compression test. What is the compressive strength?
examples.idea: Compressive strength is the failure load divided by the loaded cross-sectional area of the cylinder. Newtons over square millimetres gives MPa.

examples.problem: In a tension test, a metal bar reaches a stress of 150 MPa at a strain of 0.0008, still on the straight-line part of the curve. What is the modulus of elasticity?
examples.idea: On the linear part of the stress-strain curve Hooke's law applies: stress = E × strain. The modulus of elasticity is the slope of that line and measures stiffness, not strength.

examples.problem: Using E_{c} = 4,700 × the square root of f'_{c} (both in MPa), what is the modulus of elasticity of concrete with a compressive strength of 40 MPa?
examples.idea: The stiffness of normal-weight concrete rises with the square root of its compressive strength, so doubling the strength raises the modulus by only about 41%.

examples.problem: A tension specimen has a gauge length of 50 mm. After fracture the gauge length measures 61.0 mm. What is the percent elongation?
examples.idea: Percent elongation is the permanent increase in gauge length at fracture divided by the original gauge length. It is a measure of ductility, along with reduction of area.

examples.problem: A tension specimen has an original diameter of 11.2 mm. After fracture the diameter at the neck is 8.8 mm. What is the percent reduction in area?
examples.idea: Reduction in area measures ductility: the loss of cross-section at the fracture as a percentage of the original. Areas go with diameter squared.

examples.problem: A metal has a yield strength of 310 MPa and a modulus of elasticity of 200 GPa. What is its modulus of resilience?
examples.idea: The modulus of resilience is the energy per unit volume a material can absorb without permanent deformation: the area under the straight part of the stress-strain curve, (yield strength)^{2} / (2E).

sections.deep:
The stress-strain curve summarises a material's mechanical behaviour. The initial straight line is elastic, with slope E. The yield strength marks the start of permanent deformation, the ultimate strength is the peak, and the strain at fracture measures ductility. The area under the curve is energy per unit volume: resilience up to yield, toughness up to fracture.

Steel is ductile with a clear yield; concrete and cast iron are brittle and far weaker in tension than compression. Other time-dependent behaviours matter in design: creep under sustained load, fatigue under repeated load and, for concrete, shrinkage.
method: Read the quantity asked for from the right part of the curve.
Compute E as stress over strain within the straight portion only.
Compute ductility as percent elongation or percent reduction in area.
Use the 0.2% offset method when there is no distinct yield point.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Mechanical properties describe how a material responds to load: how stiff it is, the stress at which it yields, the stress at which it breaks, and how much it stretches first. They are read from a stress-strain curve.
needs: Mechanics of Materials: Stresses and strains
leads: Structural Engineering: Design of reinforced concrete components
terms: change in length divided by original length; it has no units
the stiffness of a material: stress divided by strain while the material still springs back
the stress at which a metal stops springing back and starts to deform permanently

play.intro: Materials is 5 to 8 of the 110 exam questions. This lesson's questions: recognise the type in the left column, make the move on the right, and stay near 3 minutes each.
rows: Stress-strain curve questions
Initial slope = E; flat step = yield; peak = ultimate; area under = toughness.
Modulus or strain from a load test
Ductile versus brittle, or which material is which
Steel: long plastic range. Concrete and cast iron: brittle, strong in compression.
Corrosion, fatigue, creep
